title: Bidirectional BFS in London: Meet in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch a real-map style route search where two BFS waves start at start/end and stop the moment they meet. This “meeting in the middle” cuts the explored graph dramatically—perfect for coding interview prep.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — imagine launching TWO BFS searches at once ⚡ Ever wondered why meeting in the middle can feel like cheating?

Here’s the mechanics (visualized on Canary Wharf streets):
1) Start a BFS from the source.
2) Start a BFS from the destination (on the same graph).
3) Expand the smaller frontier each step.
4) As soon as a node appears in both visited sets, you’ve found the shortest path.

Why it’s faster:
- Regular BFS explores outward layer-by-layer from one side.
- Bidirectional BFS explores from both ends, reducing the effective depth from d to d/2 on each side.
- That usually means way fewer total nodes visited on large graphs.

Takeaway: If your graph is unweighted (or edges have uniform cost), bidirectional BFS is one of the cleanest graph optimization wins for shortest paths.

Debate Q: Should you always use bidirectional BFS in interviews, or are there cases where plain BFS still wins?
